Opportunities in Adversity  |  Tough times make brilliant businesses  |  2024  |  01. 
Entrepreneurs can easily become discouraged in the current 
turbulent environment. However, economic challenges come 
with significant opportunities. This report illustrates that 
tough times are not a barrier to entrepreneurship; rather, 
they can ignite innovation and growth. We hope this research 
highlights just some of the opportunities possible during 
periods of adversity by showcasing inspiring entrepreneurs 
and companies that can encourage others to seek out new 
opportunities. 
 
This report explores how economic hardships, including 
the 2008 global financial crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic, 
and the current recessionary environment, have fostered 
entrepreneurial opportunities in the UK. During the financial 
crisis, 585k new businesses were incorporated, in sectors 
like software and fintech—many of which are household 
names today. Similarly, the COVID-19 pandemic accelerated 
a digital shift, leading to a surge in businesses operating 
in software and mobile apps. From March 2020 to January 
2022, 1.43m new businesses were established. Success 
stories like Forest (page 11) and Muc-Off (page 13) highlight 
the benefits of flexibility and quick thinking in challenging 
times. 
 
The current recessionary environment—with high 
inflation and increased interest rates—continues to 
test entrepreneurial resilience. Despite the challenges, 
new businesses are emerging, especially in application 
software and AI—which attracted a record £3.28b in 
equity investment in 2022. Our survey reveals that 54.0% 
of business owners view the current recession as an 
opportunity. Additionally, 63.0% believe AI will boost 
productivity and efficiency, while 60.0% foresee increased 
profitability. Despite mixed feelings about the policy 
changes likely to be introduced under the new Labour 
government, the entrepreneurial spirit remains strong.  
 
At Charles Stanley, we are committed to supporting 
entrepreneurs through good times and bad. Our holistic 
approach ensures personalised financial planning and 
investment strategies tailored to long-term success and 
financial security. Despite the bumps along the way, 
adversity often fuels innovation and business formation, 
especially in tech sectors. Looking ahead, AI, clean 
technology, and digital health are poised to drive the next 
wave of entrepreneurial growth. We remain dedicated to 
guiding our clients through these emerging opportunities.

Opportunities in Adversity  |  Tough times make brilliant businesses  |  2024  |  02. 
Introduction
This report explores how various periods of economic 
hardship have created opportunities for the UK’s 
entrepreneurial ecosystem. Where others see problems, 
entrepreneurs see opportunities, meeting new demands or 
adapting their business models to better suit evolving needs. 
 
Throughout the UK’s history, several periods of economic 
hardship have shaped the economy. This report will focus 
on the global financial crisis (GFC) of 2008, the COVID-19 
pandemic, and the current cost-of-living crisis. Although 
the GFC began in the US, its fallout spread worldwide, 
significantly impacting the UK’s service-driven economy. 
 
During the GFC, 585k UK businesses were incorporated, 
with the period seeing an increase in application software 
companies and the emergence of challenger banks. 
The COVID-19 pandemic created an opportunity for 
entrepreneurs to solve the issues presented by the “new 
normal” that the pandemic created. Many businesses began 
to operate in the digital space, in sectors such as application 
software, software-as-a-service (SaaS), and mobile apps. 
COVID-19 also created a situation where companies could 
pivot their current operations to better suit the current 
climate, either by offering a new range of products or by 
changing how products and services are offered. 
 
The COVID-19 pandemic caused changes to ways of working 
that have never been witnessed before. Global lockdowns 
kept people indoors and made them more reliant than ever 
on digital services. The measures designed to help with 
recovery led to inflationary pressure, which, combined with 
external factors such as the war in Ukraine, supply chain 
complications, and an energy crisis, pushed the UK into a 
cost-of-living crisis in 2021. Each economic event created 
unique situations for entrepreneurs to overcome. With 
this came new technologies and sectors for companies to 
operate in, which are explored in this report.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Artificial intelligence (AI) offers huge opportunities for 
businesses across many sectors. It allows businesses to 
streamline their operations and creates opportunities for 
those who can identify new ways to apply the technology. 
Businesses working in AI have attracted a significant amount 
of equity investment, peaking at £3.28b in 2022.  
 
This report also features a survey of business owners 
conducted by Charles Stanley. The results suggest that UK 
business owners are optimistic about the future, viewing 
trends like global protectionism as opportunities where 
others may see threats. The survey highlights the excitement 
business owners feel about AI and its potential, as well as 
the impact that COVID-19 had on them and their businesses.

How and why Charles Stanley supports 
entrepreneurs 
At Charles Stanley, we offer a comprehensive suite of 
services designed to meet the needs of entrepreneurs at 
every stage of their journey. We support entrepreneurs 
because they are the backbone of a healthy economy. 
Entrepreneurs drive innovation, bring new products and 
services to market, and create employment opportunities. 
Our goal is to empower them to succeed, which, in turn, fuels 
economic progress. Our 200-year history means we have had 
to deal with adversity, from economic disasters to wars, and 
all the while, we have continued to support entrepreneurs.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
From the start of our relationship, we will take the time to 
listen and understand your journey, your hopes, goals, and 
fears. We will offer you long-term support, we know that 
your needs will change over time. We work in synergy with 
legal, tax, and accountancy teams meaning we can build 
your investment portfolios that reflect your financial needs 
and lifestyle, aiming to ensure the highest level of integrated 
client service. We work with your tax adviser to maximise 
your tax efficiency across income, capital gains, and 
inheritance tax. Our team of advisers can also help you plan 
a business exit or transfer. We will structure your wealth 
flexibly, freeing your time to focus on personal ambitions, 
your family, and the big picture of your business strategy. 
Our wealth management service involves dedicated financial 
planners and investment managers who will provide you 
with a holistic financial plan and personalised investment 
strategy. We will explore your financial requirements to 
create a plan that meets your goals, gives you confidence 
in your investment strategy, and forms a secure financial 
future for you and your loved ones.  
 
For entrepreneurs seeking professional investment 
management, our bespoke investment service offers 
dedicated experts to handle your investments. You’ll have 
direct contact with your investment manager, who will 
build a portfolio tailored to your personal circumstances, 
investment objectives, and risk appetite. This service can 
also accommodate specific preferences, such as responsible 
and ESG investing. 
 
Our commitment to entrepreneurs extends beyond 
investment management. We offer holistic financial planning 
services that address various life stages and significant 
events—including inheritance, divorce or retirement—
ensuring you and your family achieve financial security. Our 
range of planning tools and techniques can also help you 
become more tax-efficient with your savings.

Timeline of UK economy (2008-2024)
Since the 2008 global financial crisis, the UK 
economy has navigated significant turbulence, 
affecting both large and small businesses. After 63 
consecutive quarters of growth, the UK’s economy 
contracted for five quarters, taking until 2013 to 
return to its pre-crisis size.1 As a service-driven 
economy, the UK is deeply impacted by fluctuations 
in both domestic and international spending. Reduced 
consumer and business spending during economic 
downturns amplifies job losses across critical sectors 
such as retail, finance, and hospitality.  
 
Unemployment peaked at 8.50% at the end of 2011, 
underlining the lasting economic strain.2 The post-
GFC recovery was further hampered by stagnant 
productivity levels, which have remained low even 
before the Brexit uncertainties began affecting 
company investment in capital expenditure, 
personnel, and training.  
 
Uncertainty following the Brexit referendum 
and the UK’s subsequent departure from the EU 
only intensified economic challenges. Then the 
COVID-19 pandemic delivered a sharp, sudden 
blow to operational norms and economic stability. 
In response, the UK government implemented 
significant interventions, including interest rate cuts 
and quantitative easing, to buffer the economy and 
support businesses. 
 
These measures led to inflationary pressures, 
prompting the Bank of England to later increase 
interest rates, dampening growth and directing 
investment away from riskier assets such as private 
equity and venture capital.  
 
Despite these challenges, there are emerging signs 
of recovery—at least for the equity investment 
market. Recent signals from the Bank of England 
suggest potential rate cuts and positive growth 
forecasts from major UK banks indicate improving 
conditions for SMEs. 
 
The general election in July 2024 resulted in a win 
for the Labour Party. It is the first time in 14 years 
the party has been in power. Labour is planning to 
increase the minimum wage and set up Great British 
Energy, among other improvements to the NHS and 
education. These policies will aim to lift the UK out of 
its current period of economic hardship.

UK business owners are optimistic about the future, seeing 
opportunities in AI, diversity, hybrid working, falling inflation, 
and even global protectionism.  
 
The COVID-19 pandemic brought mixed outcomes for 
business owners. More businesses (32.0%) emerged from 
the pandemic stronger than those that almost failed (20.0%). 
For businesses that started post-COVID-19, 35.0% of owners 
gained the confidence to start their business, 33.0% found 
the time to start it, 19.0% secured the finance, and 27.0% 
saw opportunities directly due to the pandemic. 
 
AI is already impacting businesses, with 52.0% of owners 
using it professionally. Most owners (63.0%) believe AI will 
improve productivity and efficiency, and 60.0% think it will 
increase profitability.  
 
With the new Labour government now elected, businesses 
are preparing for the party’s potential policy changes. Most 
(53.0%) think an increased minimum wage would benefit 
their business, and 43.0% feel positive about changes to 
immigration policy. However, 50.0% say increased business 
tax would have a negative impact on their company. Labour 
have now claimed that corporation tax will not change.

Companies incorporated during GFC  
(2007 Q4-2009 Q2)
The collapse of the US financial system in 2008 sent 
shockwaves across the globe, triggering widespread 
economic downturn, a rise in unemployment, and five 
consecutive quarters of negative growth for the UK 
economy.3 Although all G7 economies fell into recession in 
2008, the UK was the last to exit.4 Service-driven industries 
such as finance, real estate, and retail were hit hardest 
by the GFC. Compared to other G7 economies, the UK 
relies more on service industries. As a result, the impacts 
of the GFC lasted longer. While the GFC of 2008 rocked 
economies, there was a silver lining—it fuelled a surge in 
entrepreneurship.5 
 
The GFC highlighted the resilience and perseverance 
of entrepreneurs in the UK and their ability to rise from 
adversity. Between 2007 Q4 and 2009 Q2, a total of 585k 
UK businesses were incorporated, of which 118k (20.3%) 
are still actively operating. The survival rate of GFC-
founded businesses indicates the numerous obstacles and 
economic events they had to navigate in the years that 
followed the GFC rather than a reflection of their intrinsic 
quality. 
 
Private company incorporations increased by 16.3% 
between 2007 Q4 and 2008 Q1. The rise in company 
formations can be attributed to “entrepreneurial 
necessity”—where more individuals are motivated to create 
companies due to job scarcity and economic hardship.6 
University of Oxford spinout, Immunocore is one example 
of a business that successfully navigated the difficulties of 
the 2008-2009 financial crisis. Founded in December 2007 
by Ian Laing, Immunocore is a biotechnology company that 
develops drugs to combat autoimmune diseases. Although 
born amidst a financial crisis, the business has since raised 
more than £400m in equity investment and was listed on 
the NASDAQ stock exchange at a market capitalisation of 
$258m in February 2021.

Sectoral trends
The GFC highlighted the need for innovative and competitive 
services that could withstand a post-recession climate. The 
most popular sector for newly incorporated companies was 
application software. Businesses using application software 
create web-based programmes that can be used to perform 
tasks on the Internet. Advancements in the digital society 
spurred businesses to create novel products and services, 
capitalising on the emergence of tech-savvy consumers. 
The events of 2008-2009 saw the emergence of challenger 
banks such as Oplo and Tandem, which leveraged the 
financial crisis to offer customer-oriented financial support 
at a time when public confidence in traditional banking 
institutions waned. 
The number of businesses in distribution and wholesale 
services, property development and construction, and 
e-commerce services also increased. However, fewer 
entrepreneurs ventured into manufacturing, possibly 
contributing to a 12.3% decline in outputs between Q1 2008 
and Q2 2009.7 Similarly, the challenging economic climate 
contributed to the low rates of recruitment companies.

Case study: Tandem
Tandem operates a digital challenger bank with a particular 
focus on green finance and promoting a more sustainable 
planet. Founded in Blackpool in 2014, Tandem introduced 
a disruptive financial service that leverages technology to 
assist clients in making greener financial decisions. The 
fintech was founded by serial entrepreneur and fintech 
specialist Ricky Knox to provide customers with easy access 
to tailored financial tools, mortgages, and savings accounts.  
 
The global financial crisis highlighted the vulnerabilities of 
traditional banking and led to a decline in public confidence. 
This created market opportunities for fintech businesses 
such as Tandem, which emerged as alternative financial 
services. In contrast to traditional financial institutions, 
fintech services are more innovative and affordable 
—simplifying banking for the increasingly tech-savvy 
customer.8 The increased scrutiny of traditional banking, in 
conjunction with the rapid growth of technology, contributed 
to the popularity of challenger banks that offered innovative 
digital solutions to customers’ financial queries. Since its 
inception, Tandem has expanded across the nation with 
offices in Cardiff, London, Durham, and Manchester. It now 
employs more than 500 people and has gained the interest 
of international and UK investors, raising an impressive 
£362m in equity investment to date.  
 
Tandem’s strategic acquisitions—Oplo, Allium, Loop, and 
Harrods Bank—work with a shared vision—to help more 
people make greener decisions, helping the planet and 
their financial health. Oplo, acquired by Tandem in April 
2022, emerged from the global financial crisis. Founded 
by Alexander Mollart, who now leads Tandem as CEO, Oplo 
was established in 2009 with a clear mandate to offer more 
equitable financial services. It aimed to address the needs 
of UK customers affected by the economic fallout and 
overlooked by conventional high-street banks during the 
global crash. It has facilitated over £1.00b in responsible 
loans since its establishment.

Successes founded during COVID-19
The COVID-19 pandemic restructured economies globally—
the introduction of trade restrictions, social distancing, and 
lockdowns contributed to an economic slowdown. It presented 
measurable challenges for existing businesses, particularly for 
entrepreneurs and the high-growth ecosystem. Entrepreneurs 
play a crucial role in the economy, with small and medium 
enterprises (SMEs) accounting for 90.0% of global business and 
70.0% of employment.9  
 
Despite its challenges, the pandemic created an opportunity for 
established and aspiring entrepreneurs to solve new problems 
and develop innovative products and services to serve a post-
pandemic economy. It also created ample opportunities for 
emerging and disruptive businesses, with more individuals 
finding the time to launch their businesses. This is reflected by 
the 1.43m businesses established between March 2020 and 
January 2022. The high number of businesses incorporated 
during COVID-19 compared to the GFC reflects the growth in the 
size of the UK economy in the years since the crisis.  
 
Companies that leveraged digital technology to provide 
interactive activities and enhance customer experience 
thrived during the pandemic. Fundraising activity in 2021 
reached unprecedented levels, which can be attributed to the 
economic stimulus measures resulting from the pandemic. 
These measures encouraged investment and increased investor 
appetite for technology companies.  
 
UK businesses founded between March 2020 and January 2022 
have participated in 6.15k fundraising deals, raising £14.0b in 
equity investment and have collectively generated a turnover 
of £440b. Top fundraising deals include London-based pet 
insurance provider Many Pets, which raised £300m between 
March 2021 and January 2022.

Top sectors for high-growth companies incorporated during COVID-19 
(March 2020-January 2022)
The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated advancements in digital 
technologies. A “new normal” required significant changes to 
people’s livelihoods, and companies in many industries had 
to advance their digital offerings. Application software was 
the most popular area for new businesses during this period. 
Application software refers to digital programmes that 
can be used to perform tasks in various industries such as 
healthcare, fintech, and e-commerce. This sector was popular 
during COVID-19 because of the rise in demand for digital 
services, as operating online became increasingly necessary. 
 
Software-as-a-service (SaaS), data analytics, mobile apps, 
and online retailing were also among the top sectors for new 
businesses launched during the pandemic. SaaS businesses 
offer subscription-based software services for personal or 
business use via the Internet. Companies established during 
this time include the e-commerce platform Shop Circle. 
The London-based company develops digital software 
to help businesses increase sales and improve customer 
experience. With more businesses moving their services 
online due to COVID-19 restrictions, companies like Shop Circle 
provided an innovative solution to help businesses adjust to 
unprecedented times. Since launching in April 2021, the 
SaaS business has raised £69.3m in equity investment. 
Similarly, businesses specialising in data analytics assess 
datasets in various industries and provide actionable insights 
for their clients. For example, True Layer is a SaaS business 
that uses application software to develop APIs (application 
programming interface) for banks. The London-based firm’s 
technology allows banks to have standardised access to their 
clients’ data. At a time when physical contact was restricted, 
such solutions allowed businesses to carry on with day-to-
day activities while giving customers peace of mind.

Case study: Forest
Forest, formerly HumanForest, operates a digital mobility 
company offering e-bikes as a convenient and eco-
friendly transport option. The London-based company was 
established in 2019 by chief executive and founder  
Agustin Guilisasti and co-founders Caroline Seton and 
Michael Ackermann. Guilisasti explains that Forest was born 
with a mission to create a more sustainable environment, 
“reforesting the world, one e-bike at a time.”10 Guilisasti’s 
experiences in the Amazon inspired the creation of Forest, 
where he came to the realisation people needed greener, 
more affordable transport services as current “shared 
mobility solutions in London were too expensive, and pricing 
out ordinary people.” 11 
 
Like many businesses, Forest had to navigate and 
strategically adapt to the challenges of the COVID-19 
pandemic. Amidst the adversity caused by the global 
shutdown, Forest seized the opportunity to reiterate the 
importance of sustainable and socially-distanced mobility 
solutions. It also led to increased demand for safe, eco-
friendly transport solutions in a post-pandemic world. Forest 
launched at an opportune time, benefiting from some of the 
positive trends the pandemic encouraged.  
 
Amid the economic uncertainties that resulted from 
the COVID-19 pandemic, Forest remained committed to 
affordability, ensuring that e-bikes remained accessible to all 
people. The business strategically used the resulting cost-
of-living crisis as an opportunity to provide a more affordable 
mobility solution to the general public. This is underscored 
by co-founder and Head of Growth Caroline Seton, who 
highlights that “affordable micromobility has the ability to 
address both environmental and financial questions that are 
prominent in today’s environment.”12 The e-company combines 
micromobility with digital marketing and partnerships to 
drive its mission forward and remain affordable. Forest has 
forged collaborations with sustainable corporates, such as 
Pangaia and Nutmeg. Digital partnerships with like-minded 
businesses allow the e-bike company to remain affordable 
and offer a competitive edge by providing businesses with 
access to their customer base while maintaining affordable 
prices for their customers.  
 
Since its inception, the business has raised a total of £17.4m 
in equity investment, with support from backers including 
Triodos Bank and crowdfunding platform Crowdcube. In 
its latest equity fundraising round (November 2023), the 
business raised £5.00m to develop its advertising technology 
platform, which displays brand advertising that helps Forest 
reduce the cost of renting its e-bikes. This raise reflects 
continued investor confidence, even as the world settles into 
a post-pandemic era.

Opportunities in Adversity  |  Tough times make brilliant businesses  |  2024  |  13. 
Established in 1994, Muc-Off initially developed cleaning 
products specifically for bicycles. Over time, the company 
expanded its product line to include maintenance solutions 
for motorcycles and cars. Based in Dorset, Muc-Off was 
founded by Rex and Marilyn Trimnell and has remained a 
family-owned business. The company’s clientele includes 
professional cycling teams, motorsports teams, and 
automotive companies. As the official supplier of Bicycle 
Care Products to Team Sky, Muc-Off has collaborated 
closely with this elite cycling team to innovate and develop 
new technologies aimed at enhancing bike performance and 
efficiency.  
 
As the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted supply chains and 
changed consumer behaviours, Muc-Off introduced a new 
range of sanitation and personal protective equipment 
to meet the increased demand for hygiene products. The 
company launched antibacterial sanitisers and cleaners 
tailored to address consumers’ concerns about virus 
transmission. This expansion not only broadened Muc-Off’s 
product portfolio but allowed the company to engage 
with customers beyond its traditional cycling and motor 
enthusiast base.  
 
 
Muc-Off’s CEO, Alex Trimnell, son of Rex and Marilyn, 
describes the pivot as a necessary response to an 
unprecedented situation. “After planning for growth, the 
pandemic forced us to focus on how to survive and protect 
our employees’ livelihood,” says Trimnell.15 “The pandemic 
highlighted the immediate need for hand sanitisers. We saw 
an opportunity to support this by helping distilleries bottle 
their products. Once we were able to source alcohol we 
started producing sanitiser ourselves.”16 Muc-Off received 
an Innovate UK grant in 2020 to aid in the development of a 
deployable sanitiser mini-bottling plant.  
 
Trimnell also noted a significant development in the cycling 
industry during the pandemic. While other European 
countries imposed bans on cycling, the UK did not, which 
inadvertently led to an increase in its popularity. This surge 
benefited Muc-Off’s traditional product lines as more 
people turned to cycling for exercise and transportation 
during lockdowns, leading to greater demand for bicycle 
maintenance products.  
 
By leveraging its expertise in product development and 
manufacturing, Muc-Off maintained its operational stability 
and even found growth opportunities amid global economic 
uncertainties.

pandemic, were all driving factors in the rise in inflation.

shown remarkable resilience, continuing to create new 
businesses. The prevalence of high-growth companies in 
the application software industry reflects a broader pattern

companies are also in the AI industry, aligning with the

companies still active from this period is more a reflection 
of the limited time they have had to fail rather than an

The potential of AI for businesses
AI is revolutionising business operations across a range of 
industries, including manufacturing, healthcare, and finance. 
AI technology offers companies the ability to expand their 
offerings and streamline operations, which leads to overall 
increases in efficiency. While some fear the impact AI will 
have, 62.0% of business owners are excited about what AI 
will bring and 60.0% think it will make their business more 
profitable, helping dispel the myths of the danger of AI and 
instead demonstrating that many business owners view it as 
an opportunity.  
 
The AI sector is fertile ground for funding, with companies in 
the sector attracting significant equity investment over the 
past ten years. Equity investment encourages AI companies 
to conduct research and development, an important 
factor for innovation. The value of equity investment in AI 
companies peaked in 2022 at £3.28b, up 10.4% from the 
previous year. The high investment amounts seen in 2021 
and 2022 are partly a result of the economic stimulus 
measures introduced to help companies recover from the 
COVID-19 pandemic. However, these investment amounts 
also reflect investor’s confidence in the future of this 
emerging sector. Investment amounts fell in 2023, in line 
with what we have seen in the high-growth tech industry, 
while deal numbers maintained the high levels seen 
throughout 2021 and 2022.

Case study: Samudra Oceans 
Samudra Oceans, co-founded by Joyeeta Das and  
Alexander Facey, uses artificial intelligence technology 
and robotics to advance seaweed farming, focusing on 
sustainable practices and blue carbon credits. Blue carbon 
credits are environmental credits that companies or 
individuals can purchase to offset their carbon emissions. 
These credits fund the conservation and restoration of 
coastal ecosystems like mangroves, salt marshes, and 
seagrass meadows, which are potent in capturing and 
storing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Based in 
London, the company aims to leverage the potential of 
seaweed for carbon capture and storage, as it captures 
significantly more carbon per unit area than terrestrial 
forests.
 
Samudra Oceans has developed a range of AI-powered 
monitoring systems and robotics designed to streamline 
the process of seaweed farming. These technologies 
aim to reduce the labour-intensive aspects of subsea 
farming and lower overhead costs such as manual labour 
and fuel. The developed system provides real-time data 
directly to farmers, allowing for more precise monitoring 
of water conditions and seaweed growth. This is crucial 
for maintaining the health and productivity of the crops. In 
addition to its technological initiatives, Samudra Oceans 
engages in research partnerships with marine biologists and 
environmental scientists to enhance its AI algorithms. These 
partnerships help refine predictions of growth patterns to 
optimise seaweed cultivation.  
 
Beyond environmental benefits, Samudra Oceans also 
focuses on the economic viability of seaweed farming. By 
making the technology affordable and easy to use, the 
company aims to empower coastal communities worldwide.  
 
Currently, Samudra Oceans operates in the UK and has 
projects in Jamaica, with plans to expand into India and 
Sri Lanka. The company has secured investments from 
the British Design Fund, which has contributed to its pre-
seed funding rounds. These funds have been used to build 
and deploy more prototypes in additional regions. To date, 
Samudra Ocean has raised £920k via two fundraising rounds.

Opportunities in Adversity  |  Tough times make brilliant businesses  |  2024  |  17. 
The history of entrepreneurship in the UK demonstrates 
that adversity often breeds opportunity. This report has 
highlighted how periods of economic hardship, such 
as the GFC of 2008 and the COVID-19 pandemic, have 
spurred a wave of innovation and new business formations. 
Software took off following the GFC as software provided 
opportunities for cash-strapped businesses to do more 
with less. A similar trend played out during the pandemic 
when technology played an outsize role in the lives of 
those living through lockdowns in the UK and working from 
home. So, despite the challenges, tough times have proven 
fertile ground for entrepreneurial ventures, particularly in 
technology-driven sectors. 
 
The current challenging moment for the UK economy may 
be the proving ground for the next generation of promising 
UK companies. The Charles Stanley survey findings 
reveal that UK entrepreneurs remain optimistic, seeing 
potential even in the current environment. Most business 
owners (54%) view the current recession as an opportunity 
for entrepreneurship, and 63% believe AI will improve 
productivity and efficiency. The proposed policy changes 
by the newly elected Labour government have a mixed 
effect on businesses owners, with an increase in minimum 
wage viewed positively but some are fearful of the impact 
of potential changes to taxation. The rise of AI represents 
the next frontier, promising to transform industries and 
create new business opportunities. Additionally, sectors 
like clean technology and digital health are emerging as 
significant areas of focus. Case studies such as Tandem, 
Forest, and Samudra Oceans illustrate the resilience and 
creativity of businesses that have not only survived but 
thrived by addressing emerging needs and leveraging new 
technologies. 
 
While tough times test businesses’ mettle, they also catalyse 
innovation and growth. Economic disruption and political 
change present opportunities for those who can move 
quickly. Entrepreneurs who can navigate these challenges 
and seize the opportunities presented are likely to drive the 
next wave of economic development in the UK.
